715.title: The harp (1 Samuel 16:14–23)
715.hook: young David plays, and the troubled king is refreshed
715.howItsDone: Christians sing and play music as part of worship, and some point to David playing for Saul when they talk about music as comfort for the troubled.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eliab, passed over, and your line was god looks on the heart.

Yesterday ended with the Spirit of the LORD coming upon David. The very next verse: "But the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD troubled him." One young man filled. One king emptied, and tormented. Nothing says Saul's servants know about the oil in Bethlehem. What they can see is that their king is not well. Find a man who can play the harp, they say, and when the trouble comes on you, he'll play with his hand, "and thou shalt be well."

Start with the hard phrase: an evil spirit from the LORD. Readers have wrestled with it. Some understand it as a real spiritual being that God permits to trouble Saul. Others read it as the text's way of saying that Saul's own darkness, his fear and his rage, became a kind of judgment. Some modern readers hear something like deep anguish or depression, though the text doesn't use our words, and gives no diagnosis. Whatever it is, it comes in waves, and it hurts. Then one servant names a name: "I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, that is cunning in playing." Brave, he adds, a man of war, prudent, comely, and the LORD is with him. So Saul sends to Jesse: "Send me David thy son, which is with the sheep." The anointed boy walks into the court of the king he'll replace, with a donkey laden with bread, a bottle of wine and a young goat from his father. The text says Saul loves him greatly and makes him his armor bearer. Nothing in the text says Saul knows who he's hired. The Hebrew word for the instrument is kinnor, a stringed instrument; the King James says harp, and some modern translations say lyre. Then the chapter's last verse: "when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him." Refreshed. No speech, no fix for what was wrong. Just a boy, a few strings, and a tormented man able to breathe again, for now.
screen: `CUNNING IN PLAYING, AND THE LORD WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: If you can, put on one quiet piece of music, play something yourself, or hum; if you can't, listen to the quietest sounds around you as if they were music. If you pray, the Psalms are there to borrow. Music can help, but when the trouble is heavy it isn't the only help, and reaching for a person is part of the cure too.
The harp. David's kinnor in Saul's court. When the trouble came on the king, David played with his hand, and Saul was refreshed, and was well.
Your line: music can heal. Saul was refreshed, and was well, for a time. See you tomorrow.

716.title: Five smooth stones (1 Samuel 17)
716.hook: a shepherd refuses the king's armor and faces the giant with a sling
716.howItsDone: Christians tell the story of David and Goliath to children and adults alike, and read David's words, I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, as trust in God rather than in weapons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the harp, and Saul refreshed. Your line was music can heal.

Two armies on two hills, a valley between, and morning and evening a champion walks out: Goliath of Gath, in a helmet of brass and a coat of mail, with a spear like a weaver's beam. "I defy the armies of Israel this day; give me a man, that we may fight together." Nobody goes. Saul and all Israel are dismayed, and greatly afraid. A shepherd boy arrives from Bethlehem with grain and loaves for his brothers, and cheeses for their captain. He asks who this Philistine is, "that he should defy the armies of the living God?" His eldest brother, Eliab, the one Samuel almost anointed, is furious. The question reaches the king.
screen: `A BOY WITH LOAVES FOR HIS BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: Saul says what anyone would: "Thou art not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him: for thou art but a youth." David answers with his résumé, and it's all sheep. A lion took a lamb; he went after it. A bear too. "The LORD that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine." Saul does the kindest thing he knows. He dresses David in his own armor: helmet of brass, coat of mail, his sword. Saul stood higher than any of the people, and some readers point out he was the obvious one to face the giant. Instead he hands his gear to a boy. David tries to walk in it, and stops: "I cannot go with these; for I have not proved them. And David put them off him." The armor isn't bad. It's Saul's, and David has never fought in it. He takes what he has tested: "he took his staff in his hand, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd's bag." His sling in his hand. The text never says why five. Mocked, David answers, "Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts." One stone sinks into the giant's forehead, and he falls on his face. Then, quietly: "there was no sword in the hand of David." Saul's sword was left behind with the borrowed armor.
screen: `THE LION, THE BEAR, AND THIS PHILISTINE.`
`NO SWORD IN THE HAND OF DAVID.`

segments.voice: Name one giant you're facing, a hard conversation, a fear, and notice whose armor you've been wearing for it. Then ask what's already in your bag, what you've tested, patience, humor, honesty, and choose one, the way David chose a stone. If you pray, bring the giant before God.
Sling. The shepherd's weapon that sent one of five smooth stones into the giant's forehead.
Your line: not in saul's armor. David went with what he had tested. Day seven hundred sixteen.

717.title: Jonathan's love (1 Samuel 18:1–4; 20)
717.hook: the king's son gives David his robe and sword, and warns him with arrows
717.carry: a friend closer than a brother
717.howItsDone: Some Christians point to David and Jonathan as a picture of loyal friendship, and the story is read in sermons and small groups about friendship, loyalty and keeping promises.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sling: David went out with his own tested stones, not Saul's armor. Your line was not in Saul's armor.

A robe. A sword. A bow. A belt. The giant is dead, and the shepherd boy who killed him stands before King Saul, still holding the head, answering questions about his father. Somewhere in that room is the king's son, Jonathan, a soldier himself and the king's heir. And before anyone has worked out what David will mean to this family, Jonathan takes off his own robe and hands it over. Then his garments. Then his sword, his bow and his belt.
screen: `A ROBE, A SWORD, A BOW, A BELT.`

segments.voice: Chapter eighteen opens, in the King James Bible: "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Knit, like two threads worked into one cloth. Then the gift: "Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David, and his garments, even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle." A prince's robe. A prince's weapons. Some readers see the heir quietly handing his rival the signs of the throne, long before anyone says it out loud. Then the friendship is tested. Saul wants David dead, and Jonathan is caught between his father and his friend. In chapter twenty they set up a signal. Jonathan will go to a field to practice with his bow, with a boy to fetch the arrows. If he calls that the arrows are on this side, David is safe. If they are beyond, David must run. The day comes. Jonathan shoots and calls out: "Is not the arrow beyond thee?" It's a warning, and a goodbye. When the boy has gone, David comes out of hiding; they kiss one another and weep, and David weeps the most. Jonathan sends him off in peace, with the promise they made in the name of the Lord, binding them and their children after them. Proverbs has a line that fits: "there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother." Some Christians who teach on friendship turn to these two: a friendship that cost something.

Bring to mind one friend who has stood with you when it cost them, and stay with their face for a moment. Then choose one thing that's really yours to give them, not leftovers: a book you love, an hour of your time, a word of thanks you've never said. If you pray, hold that friend before God in silence; if not, simply think of them with thanks.
Jonathan's love. The king's son, knit to David soul to soul, who gave away his robe and sword and warned his friend with an arrow.
Your line: a friend closer than a brother. Two souls, knit together, and a promise that reached their children. See you tomorrow.

718.title: The cave (1 Samuel 24)
718.hook: David could kill Saul while he sleeps, and cuts only the edge of his robe
718.carry: I will not lift my hand
718.howItsDone: Some Christians read David sparing Saul in the cave alongside Jesus's teaching to love one's enemies, and the story is told in sermons and Sunday schools about refusing revenge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonathan's love: a robe, a sword, an arrow shot beyond a boy. Your line was a friend closer than a brother.

David and his men are crouched in the back of a cave in the wilderness of En-gedi, among the wild goats' rocks. Outside, King Saul is hunting him with an army. Then the king himself walks in, alone, to relieve himself, with no idea who is sitting in the dark behind him. One of David's men whispers what they're all thinking: this is the day the Lord promised, your enemy delivered into your hand. Do to him whatever seems good to you. David gets up. He creeps forward with a blade.

He cuts off a corner of Saul's robe. That's all. The king walks back into the light and never feels it. Then a strange line, in the King James Bible: "David's heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt." Not for sparing him. For the cloth. Even that small cut felt like too much. He stops his men cold: "The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD's anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him." Anointed is the key word. Saul was anointed king with oil, and David will not be the one to remove him, even after spears thrown at his head, even with a promise of the throne. Then David does something brave. He walks out after Saul and calls to him. He bows to the ground and holds up the corner of the robe as proof: I was close enough to kill you, and I didn't. "I will not put forth mine hand against my lord; for he is the LORD's anointed." He leaves the judging to God. And Saul, the hunter, breaks: "Is this thy voice, my son David? And Saul lifted up his voice, and wept." He says it plainly: "Thou art more righteous than I." It doesn't last; Saul will hunt David again. What the cave shows is a man with every excuse and every chance, choosing not to take it. Some Christians read this chapter beside Jesus's teaching to love enemies and Paul's line in Romans about leaving vengeance to God.

Let someone who has wronged you come to mind, and notice the chance you have to get even: a remark you could repeat, a favor you could withhold. Then picture David lowering his hand, holding only a scrap of cloth; you don't have to forgive everything today, just decide not to cut. If you pray, you can hand the judging to God in silence.
The cave. In the dark at En-gedi, David spares the king who is hunting him, and takes only the corner of his robe.
Your line: I will not lift my hand. A corner of cloth was all David took. Day seven hundred eighteen, done.

719.title: Abigail (1 Samuel 25)
719.hook: a wise woman rides out with bread and figs and talks David out of revenge
719.howItsDone: Some Christians tell Abigail's story as an example of courageous peacemaking and wise speech, and it is read in Bible studies about anger, conflict and the gift of a wise friend.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cave, where David spared the king hunting him. Your line was I will not lift my hand.

David spared a king in a cave. Here he nearly kills a farmer over a rude reply. The farmer is Nabal, a rich man with three thousand sheep, shearing them in Carmel. David's men have kept Nabal's shepherds safe out in the fields, and now David sends ten young men to ask, politely, for whatever Nabal can spare for a feast day. Nabal sneers. Who is David? There are plenty of runaway servants these days. Why should I give my bread to men I don't know? David gives one order: every man, gird on your sword. About four hundred of them set out.

One of Nabal's servants runs to his wife, Abigail. The text calls her a woman of good understanding, and her husband churlish and evil in his doings. She loads donkeys: two hundred loaves, two bottles of wine, five sheep ready dressed, parched corn, a hundred clusters of raisins and two hundred cakes of figs. She sends them ahead, rides after them, and tells Nabal nothing. On a hillside path she meets David coming down with his army. She gets off her donkey, bows to the ground, and takes the blame on herself. Her husband, she says, is just like his name: "as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him." Then the thing David needs to hear: when you are king one day, don't let this be a stumbling block on your conscience, that you shed blood without cause and avenged yourself with your own hand. She isn't only saving her household. She's saving David from himself. And he hears it, in the King James Bible: "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me: And blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand." He blesses God for sending her, her advice, and her. In the cave, David held himself back. Here someone else had to, and he was humble enough to let her. Later in the chapter Nabal dies, and David asks Abigail to be his wife.

Picture someone near you riding down the hill with their sword on, like a friend about to send an angry message. Think the way Abigail did, not how to win the argument but what would help them see their better self: bread first, words second. If you pray, ask for her kind of wisdom in your own words.
Abigail. Nabal's wise wife, who rode out with bread and figs and turned David back from shedding blood.
Your line: blessed be your wisdom. One woman on a path kept a king's hands clean. That's day seven hundred nineteen.

720.title: How are the mighty fallen (2 Samuel 1)
720.hook: David weeps for Saul, who hunted him, and for Jonathan
720.carry: swifter than eagles, stronger than lions
720.howItsDone: Some Christians read David's lament for Saul and Jonathan as a model of honest grief, and lines from it are sometimes read at funerals and memorials.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abigail on the hillside path, who kept David from avenging himself. Your line was blessed be your wisdom.

A man runs into David's camp with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. He comes from the battle on Mount Gilboa, carrying a crown and a bracelet. Saul's. The king is dead, he says, and Jonathan with him. Saul hunted David through caves and wilderness. Now the throne is open, and a man in David's position might feel relief. Instead David takes hold of his own clothes and tears them, and so do all the men with him. They mourn, and weep, and fast until evening, for Saul, for Jonathan, and for the people. Then David sings.

The song is a lament, and the text says it is written in the book of Jasher. Its refrain, in the King James Bible: "The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places: how are the mighty fallen!" He doesn't want the news spread among the enemy: "Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon." He curses the mountains where they fell. And then he praises Saul. Not a word about the spears, the caves, the running. He tells the women of Israel to weep over Saul, who clothed them in scarlet. He sings of the two together: "Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions." Some readers call it generous. Some call it political: a new king honoring the old one. The text doesn't settle it. What it does is let David grieve the whole man, the king he was, not only the enemy he became. Then the song turns personal: "I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful." Two kinds of grief sit side by side: clean grief for a friend, and tangled grief for someone who did harm, and was also brave, and was also family. The refrain comes back at the end: how are the mighty fallen. One song, big enough to hold both.
screen: `A LAMENT, WRITTEN IN THE BOOK OF JASHER.`
`DAVID PRAISES THE MAN WHO HUNTED HIM.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind whose loss is tangled: someone who hurt you and also gave you something, or someone gone you never quite made peace with; if no one comes, choose someone whose life you're grieving while they're alive. Don't tidy them up; let both be true, and find one honest good thing to say about them, as David did. If you pray, hold them before God without a verdict.
Jasher. The book that preserved David's lament for Saul, who hunted him, and for Jonathan, who loved him.
Your line: swifter than eagles, stronger than lions. One song for a friend and for a foe. Until tomorrow.

721.hook: the king dances with all his might, and his wife is embarrassed
721.tomorrow: A seat at the king's table
721.howItsDone: Some churches point to David dancing before the ark when they welcome dance, clapping and raised hands in worship, while others read it mainly as a lesson about humility and the heart behind worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, swifter than eagles, stronger than lions: David's song for Saul and Jonathan. This week walked from a harp and five stones to a crown.

Six paces. That's how far the bearers carry it before David sacrifices oxen and fatlings, the King James says. David is king now, bringing the ark of God, the sacred chest of the covenant, up into Jerusalem, his new city. And out ahead of everyone, the king is not walking with dignity. He's leaping and dancing, the text says, in a plain linen garment. Above the street, at a palace window, one person is watching who is not dancing at all: his wife Michal, the daughter of Saul.

Here is the verse: "And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod." With all his might. The King James uses the same English words for Samson bringing down the pillars, though the Hebrew behind them differs; here they describe a king's joy. The linen ephod was a simple garment, the kind the boy Samuel wore while serving at the sanctuary. The text says nothing here of a king's robe, and some readers see a king dressed for service, not for show. Then the window: "Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart." It's easy to make Michal the villain, and the text is fairer than that. She loved David once. She saved his life by letting him down through a window. Then she was given to another man while David was away, and brought back later. Her father and brothers are dead. She has her own reasons to watch from a window. But when she meets David, she mocks him for uncovering himself before the servant girls like a fool. David answers: it was before the LORD. "I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight." Sillier still, if that's what worship takes. Some Christians read this as permission for joy that looks undignified: hands raised, clapping, dancing in church. Others hear a quieter point about the heart: what matters is who the dance is for. Either way, the king forgot to look like a king.

If you can stand, stand; if not, stay where you are, and let a song with joy in it play in your head. Move something, your hands, your feet, small and silly is fine, without checking how it looks. If you pray, make it a dance before God, as David did; if you don't, let it be a dance of thanks for being alive today.
Ephod. The plain linen garment David wore as he leapt and danced with all his might before the ark.
Your line: with all his might. Michal watched; David danced anyway. A week of David, and day seven hundred twenty-one.
